title: Robert Pattinson Trolled by U.K. Government in Youth Employment Scheme Post After Bond Reveal: He’ll ‘Apply for All 90,000 Jobs’
description: Since Robert Pattinson was unveiled as James Bond, social media has been awash in jokes about how the seemingly over-employed star — who also plays
body:
Since Robert Pattinson was unveiled as James Bond, social media has been awash in jokes about how the seemingly over-employed star — who also plays Batman, was recently in “The Odyssey” and is currently on screens in “Primetime” — is coming for every job going (yes, even yours).

	Now the stiff-upper-lip types in the British government are getting in on the act. After all, Pattinson effectively works for them now as an agent of MI6.
	

	In a post on its official account on Wednesday, the government sought to raise awareness of a newly announced youth employment initiative. The scheme is expected to help get more than 90,000 young people across the U.K. into work.

	But, taking a slight detour from its usual serious tone, the government chose to highlight the initiative with a picture of Pattinson in his now-iconic Bond reveal photo, alongside the headline: “Robert Pattinson to apply for all 90,000 jobs created for young people through youth employment scheme.”


	The government’s trolling of Pattinson is just the latest addition to a growing pile of memes about the star’s uncanny ability to keep adding to his already bulging portfolio of roles. Among the lines doing the rounds are: “AI won’t take my job. Robert Pattinson will,” “If you have a job right now, that’s because Robert Pattinson doesn’t want it,” and “I’m scared to go into the office tomorrow and find Robert Pattinson already sitting at my desk.”

	As it happens, Pattinson was joking about his appetite for taking other people’s jobs long before Bond came his way.
	

	In a comment that has since resurfaced, he was asked in a 2025 Vanity Fair interview with Jennifer Lawrence about returning to the “Twilight” franchise. “I like taking jobs off younger actors. I do. I wanna play 17 again,” he said.

schema.headline: Robert Pattinson Trolled by U.K. Government in Youth Employment Scheme Post After Bond Reveal: He’ll ‘Apply for All 90,000 Jobs’

title: Elon Musk Has Invested in Skydance, David Ellison Confirms: ‘To Have Him as a Shareholder Is an Honor’
description: David Ellison, chairman and CEO of Skydance, confirmed that tech mogul Elon Musk has invested in the company, formed from the merger of Paramount a
body:
David Ellison, chairman and CEO of Skydance, confirmed that tech mogul Elon Musk has invested in the company, formed from the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery.

	Musk, the world’s richest person, invested about $1 billion in Skydance post-merger, CNBC and Semafor reported last month. Ellison, speaking Wednesday at the New York Times’ 2026 DealBook Summit at Manhattan’s Jazz at Lincoln Center, acknowledged that Musk is a part-owner of Skydance but he did not confirm the investment amount.
	

	The New York Times’ Andrew Ross Sorkin asked Ellison about the reports of Musk investing a billion dollars into Skydance, “and I think some people wanted to know whether this is the beginning of something bigger with Starlink long-term, or is a one-off as a given his relationship with your father,” Larry Ellison.

	Ellison responded, “So look, I have so much admiration and respect for Elon. I mean, I don’t know if you saw recently, but but but literally watching you know Starship, it’s a marvel…. I mean, he is both the [Nikola] Tesla and [Thomas] Edison… He is the from my perspective he is the greatest entrepreneur of our time, and he doesn’t invest in a lot of companies.” 

	Ellison continued, “So to have his vote of confidence and to have him as a shareholder is an honor and a privilege. And if there was any opportunity to be able to collaborate with him in the future… that is the appropriate opportunity in the future, we’d be thrilled to do so. But there’s nothing [right now].” 

	Ellison’s Paramount Skydance closed its $111 billion megamerger with Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct. 6, with major backing from his father, Larry Ellison. The company, one of the biggest media and entertainment conglomerates in the industry, has around $80 billion in net debt and is expected to lay off thousands of employees as part of achieving $6 billion in annualized savings by 2029.

title: Agatha Christie Series ‘Tommy & Tuppence’ Coming to Channel 5 in the U.K.
description:

	The six-part drama will be available to stream and
body:
BritBox‘s Agatha Christie series “Tommy & Tuppence” has found a home in the U.K. on Channel 5.

	The six-part drama will be available to stream and watch live this festive season, it was announced on Wednesday. Starring Antonia Thomas and Josh Dylan, the modern take on Christie’s characters premiered in North America via BritBox this past September.

	Set in present-day London, the show follows the amateur detective duo as they “fall in love, fall out of it and tumble back in, all while solving some thrilling, entertaining mysteries along the way,” as its official synopsis reads. 
	

	“Tommy & Tuppence” also stars Imelda Staunton (“Harry Potter,” “Paddington”) as Tommy’s Aunt Ada, Nicholas Richardson (“Wu-Tang: An American Saga,” “Younger”), Charlie Condou (“Doctor Who,” “Unforgotten”), Callie Cooke (“F1,” “Cheaters”) and Chizzy Akudolu (“Little Disasters,” “The Woman in the Wall”). 

	It was written and executive produced by Phoebe Eclair-Powell (“The Road Trip,” “Harm”) with Fergus O’Brien (“Happy Valley,” “The Tourist”) and Ellie Heydon (“Outrageous,” “Trying”) directing. Stella Merz (“Miss Austen,” “Gentleman Jack”) serves as producer. The show hails from Lookout Point, part of BBC Studios, and was produced in association with Agatha Christie Limited.

	“’Agatha Christie’s Tommy & Tuppence’ brings together everything audiences love about a great mystery: clever plotting, intriguing characters and plenty of twists along the way,” said Cherry Vantreen, acquisitions and co-production director at 5. “With its charming central duo and blend of suspense, adventure and wit, it’s a fantastic addition to 5’s drama offering, and we’re delighted to be bringing this classic Agatha Christie title to our viewers.”
	

	Added Eclair-Powell: “I’m so excited to see ‘Agatha Christie’s Tommy & Tuppence’ coming to Channel 5. Tommy and Tuppence are two of Christie’s most entertaining and dynamic creations, and bringing their wit, warmth and sense of adventure to the screen has been an incredible experience. I’m delighted that new audiences will have the chance to discover their world of mystery, intrigue and romance.”

	The series was executive produced by Katie Draper, Louise Mutter, Laura Lankester and Juliette Howell for Lookout Point as well as Eclair-Powell and James Prichard for Agatha Christie Limited. BBC Studios struck the deal with 5 and is handling global sales.

schema.headline: Agatha Christie Series ‘Tommy & Tuppence’ Coming to Channel 5 in the U.K.

title: ‘The Comeback King’ Trailer: Glen Powell Is a Washed-Up Country Star in Judd Apatow’s New Comedy

	The movie stars Powell as a country music star who
body:
Glen Powell and Judd Apatow‘s new comedy, “The Comeback King,” has revealed its first trailer.

	The movie stars Powell as a country music star whose career is in shambles after his pop star girlfriend, played by “Outer Banks” star Madelyn Cline, falsely claims he cheated on her. To make a comeback, he recruits the help of real-life music heavyweights including Miranda Lambert, Jelly Roll, Brad Paisley, Chris Stapleton, Megan Moroney, Shaboozey, Reba McEntire and more. The movie also features original songs performed by Powell and Cline.
	

	“The Comeback King” marks comedy king Apatow’s first movie since 2022’s pandemic spoof “The Bubble,” about a group of actors filming a movie during the height of COVID-19. The Netflix film received mostly negative reviews, and since then Apatow has executive produced a handful of documentaries and comedies, like Billy Eichner’s “Bros” and Please Don’t Destroy’s “The Treasure of Foggy Mountain.” 

	Apatow and Powell co-wrote the script for “The Comeback King,” which follows a country music star whose career is in shambles. Powell, whose star has been on the rise, previously showed off his comedy chops in movies like 2023’s rom-com hit “Anyone but You” with Sydney Sweeney and Richard Linklater’s crime comedy “Hit Man” with Adria Arjona. He’s also starred in Hulu’s “Chad Power” series, a football comedy about a washed-up quarter that’s been renewed for Season 2. Most recently, he lent his voice to Universal’s “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie” as Fox McCloud, a Nintendo crossover character, and starred in A24’s “How to Make a Killing” and Paramount’s “The Running Man” remake.
	

	“The Comeback King” cast also includes Cristin Milioti, Stavros Halkias and Li Jin Hao. The title was officially revealed earlier in April, with a photo of an oversized, very country belt buckle, and the film will release in theaters on Feb. 5.

	Watch the full “Comeback King” trailer below.

title: Steven Spielberg Calls ‘The Odyssey’ a ‘Showstopper’ and ‘One of the Greatest Things’ Matt Damon Has Ever Done
description: After a weeklong run of screening Christopher Nolan‘s “The Odyssey,” Universal saved the best for last, bringing out Steven Spielberg to moderate a
body:
After a weeklong run of screening Christopher Nolan‘s “The Odyssey,” Universal saved the best for last, bringing out Steven Spielberg to moderate a one-on-one Q&A.

	As the film ended and the house lights went up, the pair walked out to a standing ovation from an audience of about 600 guild members and voters who had come out to see the film — many on repeat viewings. 

	Before Spielberg had a moment to praise Nolan for the $1.8 billion blockbuster, it was Nolan who stepped in and humbly told Spielberg, “I just have to take a minute, because I’ve known you a long time, but I’ve never done a Q&A with you. When I was a younger man and a dear boy watching your movies, I don’t think I ever really envisioned this moment where you would be asking questions about my film.”
	

	Spielberg told Nolan he had seen the film in Imax and called it “a showstopper.” 

	When asked why now, and why he had chosen to adapt Homer’s poem, Nolan answered, “I always find it hard to figure out what to do next. Probably one of the reasons, if it’s been unpredictable, as you say, it’s because it’s always a surprise to me as well. I do one project at a time. I’m not very good at developing multiple things at the same time, so I finish one film and then I look for what might be next.”

	He continued, “What hadn’t really been done in the modern era was Greek mythology and I think the reason is because it hadn’t been done definitively. Part of the reason was because of the mythological elements; the visual effects techniques weren’t really available in the 1930s or the 1950s. When the great eras of the classical world, the world of antiquity, was big in Hollywood. ‘The Odyssey’ hadn’t been done on this scale with this movie budget, with the resources of modern technology: shooting on Imax, using visual effects and all the rest.”
	

	Nolan also talked about building his cast and choosing Matt Damon to play Odysseus. “This is one of the greatest things Matt has ever done as an actor,” Spielberg said.

	Nolan said, “Matt occurred to me right away because I’ve done two films with him in small parts. So I know from my own experience on the floor how incredible he is as an actor and how great he is to work with. How he’s just an incredible team member. He’s an incredible creative force. He’s not just thinking about his own part. He’s thinking about the whole narrative, which is a great asset. But also, he’s grown up on camera. You know, from that kid in ‘Saving Private Ryan.’ He has this ability to open up a story and take us on a journey, in empathetic terms; that’s incredibly powerful.”

	Spielberg took a moment to tell Nolan that one of his favorite scenes in the film featured Samantha Morton as the witchy goddess Circe, and he wanted to know how Nolan pulled it off. Spielberg said, “She was wonderful … That’s one of my favorite scenes in the whole movie, where they all turn into pigs.” 

	Nolan explained he didn’t want to shoot in front of a green screen or use tracking markers. “I wanted to be able to define the process.” He said he watched transformation movies such as “An American Werewolf in London” and even Neil Jordan’s “A Company of Wolves” for inspiration.

	He revealed it was a collaboration with both the visual effects and special effects departments as they navigated the challenge. “They came up with these heads that have a skull underneath that’s fractured, but it’s held together with magnets and then it’s covered in a particular type of silicone skin that looked exactly wonderfully real, but was very flexible. So we built these heads of the guys, and each take, she could go around the table and do whatever she wanted and manipulate these guys however she wanted in the most horrible ways.”

	“The Odyssey” opened in July to a $264.1 million global debut, the biggest of Nolan’s career. It has since crossed $1.8 billion, becoming his highest-grossing film. Universal and Nolan’s team are continuing to focus on the format. Nearly every Los Angeles screening is tagged Imax 70mm, 70mm or 35mm, reminding viewers that the film was shot entirely using Imax cameras and built to be judged on a screen the size of a building and not on a laptop or their home TV using the Academy digital portal.

schema.headline: Steven Spielberg Calls ‘The Odyssey’ a ‘Showstopper’ and ‘One of the Greatest Things’ Matt Damon Has Ever Done

body:
Paramount+ has dropped the first full trailer for the “Tulsa King” spinoff “Frisco King” starring Samuel L. Jackson. 

	In the trailer, Russell Lee Washington Jr. (Jackson) returns to his native New Orleans, only to find he is no longer welcome. With some advice from his friend Dwight Manfreddi (Sylvester Stallone), Washington instead sets his sights on building a criminal enterprise in suburban Frisco, TX. 


	Check out the full trailer below. 
	

	Jackson originally appeared as Washington in the third season of “Tulsa King.” The spinoff was officially ordered to series in July 2025. It is set to debut with its first two episodes on Dec. 18 on Paramount+, with new episodes dropping weekly on Fridays thereafter. 

	The official description of the series states: 

	“‘Frisco King’ follows seasoned New Orleans gangster Lee Washington as he lands in Frisco, Texas, and discovers a hustler’s playground hidden beneath the polished surface of American suburbia. Recruiting an ambitious protégé, a loyal driver, and a growing network of eccentric partners, Lee transforms small hustles into big business. But, every new score raises the stakes, and as his influence grows, so do the risks, forcing Lee to stay one grift ahead. Frisco may not know it yet, but its new king has arrived.” 

	In addition to Jackson, the series stars: Asa Germann, Kai Caster as Keith,  and Lilah Pate. Stallone also makes a special guest appearance.

	Taylor Sheridan wrote all eight episodes of “Frisco King” and serves as an executive producer along with Stallone, Jackson, David Glasser, Ron Burkle, David Hutkin, Bob Yari, Christina Alexandra Voros, Michael Friedman, LaTanya Richardson Jackson and Keith Cox. Christina Alexandra Voros and Michael Friedman both directed four episodes, with Voros directing the pilot, in addition to executive producing. The series is produced by Paramount Television Studios and 101 Studios.

title: Bruce Springsteen Concert Doc ‘When the Walls Came Down’ in the Works from Legendary Entertainment, Passion Pictures and Sony Music Vision
description: “When the Walls Came Down,” a documentary about Bruce Springsteen and The E Street Band’s 1988 East Berlin concert, is in the works from Legendary
body:
“When the Walls Came Down,” a documentary about Bruce Springsteen and The E Street Band’s 1988 East Berlin concert, is in the works from Legendary Entertainment, Passion Pictures and Sony Music Vision. 

	Nicholas de Taranto and Danielle Peck serve as co-directors and produce alongside Passion Pictures. James Marsh, the Oscar-winning director of 2008’s “Man on Wire,” serves as executive producer with Ray Sisson.


	“When the Walls Came Down” follows Springsteen from his first visit to East Berlin in 1981 to the 1988 performance and features interviews with Springsteen, Jon Landau and members of The E Street Band, including Roy Bittan, Patti Scialfa, Stevie Van Zandt and Max Weinberg. According to an official description, the Berlin show “remains the largest concert that Springsteen and The E Street Band have played in their careers. For a generation coming of age under a highly repressive Communist regime, the concert became a catalyst for change. The following year, many of those same young people would help tear the Wall itself down.”
	

	“I remember seeing the Wall and saying, ‘This isn’t right. This is an offense against humanity,’” Springsteen said. “Looking back on it, it’s in the very highest echelon of all the shows we’ve ever done. We were trying to dance with the entire country that day.”

	Marsh added, “This film explores a singular, high-stakes moment in pop culture and its incredible power over geopolitics. Bruce’s words from that night resonate now more than ever, reminding us of the enduring, unifying power of music.”

	Springsteen, the rock ‘n’ roll visionary behind “Born to Run” and “Born in the USA,” recently experienced a resurgence in the pop culture zeitgeist. The story behind his sixth studio album “Nebraska” was immortalized in Scott Cooper’s “Deliver Me From Nowhere,” which starred Jeremy Allen White as The Boss. Springsteen also recently wrapped his “Land of Hope and Dreams” American tour, which was, in part, a response to the second term of President Donald Trump, with whom Springsteen has an ongoing feud.
	

	Worldwide sales are being handled by Submarine Entertainment and Sony Music Vision.

title: Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Targets Huge Debut Above $100 Million
description:
The box office odds will certainly be in favor of “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.” 

	The latest installment in Lionsgate’s dystopian fr
body:
The box office odds will certainly be in favor of “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.” 

	The latest installment in Lionsgate’s dystopian franchise is targeting a stellar debut above $100 million from 3,900 North American theaters. Exhibitors are bullish that goodwill toward the property, as well as excitement for the return of some fan-favorite characters, could propel the opening weekend figure closer to $125 million. Should estimates hold, it’ll be one of just five movies this year to launch above $100 million, joining the elusive company of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” ($360 million), “Toy Story 5” ($159 million), “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie” ($131 million) and “The Odyssey” ($123 million).
	

	“Sunrise on the Reaping” is the sixth entry in the “Hunger Games” series, and it’s landing exactly three years after the previous chapter, 2023’s “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.” That film, a prequel starring Rachel Zegler as tribute Lucy Gray Baird and Tom Blyth as young Corolanious Snow, the future dictator of Panem, bowed to just $44 million but managed to climb to $363 million globally, making it a commercial success against a $100 million budget. The start for “Sunrise on the Reaping” should resemble the original saga, a relief for the studio since this installment carries a price tag north of $150 million. For reference, 2012’s “The Hunger Games” debuted to $152 million, with the three follow-ups, 2013’s “Catching Fire” ($158 million), 2014’s “Mockingjay Part 1” ($121 million) and 2015’s “Mockingjay Part 2” ($102 million), each hitting triple digits in opening weekend. As a franchise, “The Hunger Games” has generated more than $3.3 billion at the worldwide box office, with “Catching Fire” as the highest-grossing entry with $865 million.
	

	Based on the novel by Suzanne Collins, “Sunrise on the Reaping” takes place 25 years before the original series. It starts on the morning of the reaping of the 50th Hunger Games, known as the Second Quarter Quell, and follows Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) as he’s forced to enter the deadly arena. In “The Hunger Games,” Haymitch (Woody Harrelson) serves as a mentor to Jennifer Lawrence’s Katniss Everdeen and Josh Hutcherson’s Peeta Mellark. Francis Lawrence returned to direct, having helmed all but the first chapter in the YA-centric franchise.

	“Sunrise on the Reaping” will provide a nice jolt to the box office ahead of Thanksgiving. Then, Turkey Day should be busy for theater owners, with new offerings including Universal’s comedy “Focker in Law,” with Ariana Grande joining Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro, Disney’s animated “Hexed” and Netflix’s Imax release of “The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”

	Elsewhere this weekend, “I Play Rocky” is targeting $10 million to $13 million while expanding nationwide. The Amazon MGM movie, which depicts the real-life story of Sylvester Stallone bringing the 1976 classic “Rocky” to the big screen, has generated just under $1 million after two weekends in limited release.

	As the end of the year approaches, domestic ticket sales are impressively 20% above the same point in 2025. With potential blockbusters like “Avengers: Doomsday,” “Dune: Part Three” and “Jumanji: Open World.” on the horizon, revenues are projected to eclipse $10 billion for the first time since COVID.

title: The 100 Greatest Movie Stars of All Time
description: We all know a movie star when we see one. But how can you tell which stars shine the brightest? Measuring the greatness of a movie star can be like
body:
We all know a movie star when we see one. But how can you tell which stars shine the brightest? Measuring the greatness of a movie star can be like catching lightning in a bottle. It’s a process that requires chemistry and finesse, as well as a search for the perfect mix — that fusion of artistry and popularity, history and currency that adds up to the incandescent ideal of stardom. Not every movie star is a great actor; not every great actor is a movie star. Many of the choices on our list reflect that. Yet there’s a magic zone where talent and luminescence fuse. And there’s another overlap that might be even more important: the one between the way these people pop onscreen and the way they dance in our dreams. To choose the 100 Greatest Movie Stars, we had to use our heads, our hearts, our guts, our fantasy lives. We were looking for the stars who magnetize us, the ones who awe and overpower us and make us swoon. The ones we wish we were, and the ones who inspire the ultimate movie-star thought: “That’s who I am.”

			
			
	Henry Fonda
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				

	His signature film was, by its very narrative design, an encapsulation of his virtues as a performer: In a room of 12 angry men, you could count on him to be the calmer, quieter one, a bastion of sense and reason. Upstanding integrity may not be be the sexiest thing to be known for as a movie star, but Fonda was never stodgy with it. It’s fitting that Abraham Lincoln was one of his breakout roles, but it’s the urgently striving all-American masculinity of his Tom Joad in “The Grapes of Wrath” that really defined the Fonda aura, at least until his stubbornly humane Juror #8 came along. And the occasional, disorienting effect of his playing against type — bewildered doofus in “The Lady Eve,” ruthless villain in “Once Upon a Time in the West” — proved the strength of that type in the first place. — G.L.

	MUST SEE: “12 Angry Men”

		
			
			
	Sylvester Stallone
			
								
				

	In half a century of stardom, Sylvester Stallone has had two just roles that connected with audiences on the mythological level out of which movie stardom is sculpted. But that turned out to be just enough. The first role was, of course, Rocky Balboa, who Stallone played with hooded eyes and a voice of muffled molasses and a groggy valor that came to life. The beauty of “Rocky” is that it connected the glory of Frank Capra to the grittiness of the New Hollywood. And what made it work was the shabby majesty of Stallone’s presence, the way he believed in the character — the way he made Rocky, in his tattered dreams, an echo of us all. The second role was John Rambo, a character who critics loved in his first movie and hated in his second. Yet if “Rambo: First Blood Part II” had problematic politics, Stallone’s smoldering fury — combined with an action flair so rooted in endurance it was nearly sadomasochistic — made the character into a galvanizingly stylized pop hero. Consider “Rocky” and “Rambo” the yin and yang of a star with old movies in his (first) blood. — O.G.

	MUST SEE: “Rocky”

		
			
			
	Zendaya
			
										
					Image Credit: ©MGM/Courtesy Everett Collectio				
					
				

	You probably think that we think she became a movie star in “Dune.” Nope. It was well before that. She’s scintillating in the “Dune” films, where her stoic warrior Chani does a dance of fury around Paul Atriedes’ shifting sympathies. But the Zendaya moment that gave us that first star tingle came in a musical that never got the love or respect it deserved: “The Greatest Showman.” As she sings “Rewrite the Stars,” hanging from a hoop trapeze, her face lights up with the pleasure of knowing that a forbidden love might be stronger than prejudice. And at that moment, her joy becomes ours. Zendaya took a leap into the acting stratosphere in “Challengers,” as a tennis champ who becomes the vertex angle — now seductive, now demanding, now who’s she going to choose? — of an isosceles love triangle. She smoldered onscreen, and in “The Drama” she shored up that smolder as a vibrant bride with the darkest of secrets. Keep watching her; she’s rewriting stardom. — O.G.

	MUST SEE: “Challengers”

		
			
			
	Alain Delon
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				

	Delon was, at his peak, almost too beautiful to be a functioning movie star: unapproachably, almost icily perfect, with a flinty gaze that either conveyed tortured depths or no soul whatsoever. Yet his beauty was never merely decorative — he was fortunate to be at his most ravishing in a testy, challenging era of European cinema that knew what to do with difficult beauty. Rather than playing straightforward heroes or objects of desire, he was happy to be the statuesque psycho: a lethally yearning Tom Ripley in “Purple Noon,” a hit man whose unnerving silence is a loaded weapon in “Le Samouraï.” Even when the men he played were slightly less tortured, his unlined, fine-cut face was an ideal vessel for the ambiguities that were the stock-in-trade of filmmakers like Visconti and Antonioni. He could make action of stillness, and a character trait of mystique.     — G.L.

	MUST SEE: “Le Samouraï”

		
			
			
	Eddie Murphy
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Universal/Courtesy Everett Col				
					
				

	From the start, he’s led with his delirious effrontery. It’s there in his great characters from “Saturday Night Live” (Buckwheat, Mr. Robinson), to the point that he was practically a movie star then. When he took the literal leap in “48 Hrs.,” he became a movie star the moment you saw him singing “Roxanne” with his Walkman on. From then on for Eddie Murphy, it was “Party All the Time.” Yet from his scene-stealing role as Donkey in the “Shrek” films to the serious acclaim he earned for “Dreamgirls,” Murphy made it impossible for the entertainment industry to define him as just one thing. In the ’80s, he was the Hollywood comedy star, triumphantly irreverent in “Beverly Hills Cop” and “Coming to America,” winning the capital to make his own films his way, with all-Black casts. And starting with “The Nutty Professor,” those casts would often include Murphy in half a dozen roles, a seeming stunt that he elevated into uproarious artistry, with one guiding rule: In an Eddie Murphy movie, the more of him the better. — A.T.

	MUST SEE: “The Nutty Professor”

		
			
			
	Philip Seymour Hoffman
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Sony Pictures Classics

	Hepburn’s regal bearing, headstrong personality and ripe Mid-Atlantic diction make her easy and enjoyable to parody — Cate Blanchett won an Oscar for more or less doing just that in “The Aviator” — but her stardom was more complex and versatile than any such party trick might suggest. Many still think of Hepburn as the screen’s premier Great American Thespian, and she had the record-breaking four Oscars to prove it. (She also had an unmatched Mary Tyrone in the film version of Eugene O’Neill’s “Long Day’s Journey Into Night.”) But she was also a spry and mischievous comedian — her sweetest side brought out in her collaborations with life partner Spencer Tracy, her snappiest by onscreen soulmate Cary Grant — and, when she allowed herself to be, a delicate minimalist: See “Summertime,” one of her loveliest and most disarmingly ordinary portraits. — G.L.

	MUST SEE: “The Philadelphia Story”

		
			
			
	Jack Nicholson
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				

	The killer grin. The knitted eyebrows. The low dry singsong voice that’s like a threat turned into a seduction. The 1970s was an era of singular screen actors, but as a movie star Jack Nicholson towers over them all. Whoever he’s playing, he has a quality of cocky joy, with an anger just beneath, that turned him into something epic: the Last of the Rebels. You can trace that quality through all his performances, whether he’s rebelling against a bullying mental-ward nurse in “One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest” or the waitress who won’t give him his toast in “Five Easy Pieces” or the corruption of L.A. in “Chinatown” or his own family in “The Shining.” At heart, Nicholson is rebelling against a world that no longer has use for rebellion, and that’s what makes him so liberating. He speaks to the Last Rebel in us all. — O.G.

	MUST SEE: “One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest”

		
			
			
	Charlie Chaplin
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				

	The early 20th century was the dawn of the media age, and Chaplin towered over it in a way that’s almost hard to imagine now. For sheer iconic global popularity, he was like … well, think Cleopatra meets the Beatles meets Santa Claus. A major aspect of his celebrity is that Chaplin created himself as a storybook character: the Little Tramp, the silent-hobo-as-everyman, with his boxy mustache and bowler hat and penguin walk and gleam of innocence. He moved with the stylized wit of an angelic acrobat. Chaplin was a singular genius of physical comedy that was miraculous in its execution yet expressed a common humanity. And audiences, for the first time, saw what a movie star could be — an enchanted projection of their inner selves — as Chaplin showcased his virtuosity in a series of movies that remain touching and hilarious snapshots of the magic that launched cinema as an art form. — O.G.

	MUST SEE: “The Gold Rush”

		
			
			
	Humphrey Bogart
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				

	With his modest stature and craggy features, Bogart wasn’t the very picture of a movie star. Indeed, he was initially resigned to thuggish supporting parts, not getting to prove otherwise until he was in his 40s. But even in early vehicles like “The Petrified Forest,” he wielded a focus-pulling intensity. And once studios figured out that his gruff, retiring quality could be as quietly heroic as it was villainous, Hollywood’s most fascinatingly distinctive leading man was born: macho, wounded, surly, soulful. Perhaps his wait for A-list status accounted, in part, for the wary renegade air that was so essential to his appeal: Whether playing good guys (“Casablanca”), bad guys (“High Sierra”) or guys in the shadowy moral margins (“The Maltese Falcon”), Bogart always felt like the outsider. Which is what made him one of us. — G.L.

	MUST SEE: “Casablanca”

		
			
			
	Marilyn Monroe
			
										
					Image Credit: 20th Century Fox				
					
				

	The words “movie star” make you think of someone who’s ageless and timeless. Yet even some of the greatest stars of Old Hollywood are very much of their time. Two or three decades ago, we might have said the same thing of Marilyn Monroe. Her luscious cuddlebug sensuality was undeniable, yet it was all too easy to view her through the lens of her era: the 1950s, a period that was more than a bit peekaboo about sex.

	But then a funny thing happened. Somewhere in the middle of our own highly sexed, flagrantly explicit, seen-it-all era, the mystique of Marilyn began to grow. Rather than being trapped in her time, she started to seem more timeless than ever, as if she were the herald of our own romantic-erotic dreams. With her singular glow, her bedazzling beauty and teasing theatricality, and the incandescent enigma that runs through her performances in films from “The Seven Year Itch” to “Some Like It Hot” (the enigma: Is she a “dumb blonde,” or a smart girl doing what it takes to get by?), Marilyn had a liquid identity that pours itself into our own day and age with surprising power. As it turns out, she wasn’t trapped in her time. She was miles ahead of it.

	When you watch her in “Gentlemen Prefer Blondes” or “The Misfits,” you see that Marilyn is a far greater actress than she’s often given credit for. Yet one reason her acting chops are routinely underrated is that the mythic character she created — the persona of Marilyn — was itself a sublime performance. When she’s onscreen, whatever the role, there is something magical in the luminosity of her presence. You can’t tear your eyes (or your heart) away from her. Watching a Marilyn movie, you don’t just look at Marilyn Monroe; you melt with her. And that’s the quintessence of movie stardom. — O.G.

	MUST SEE: “Gentlemen Prefer Blondes”

title: Six Flags Magic Mountain X2 Roller Coaster Linked to Another Death
description:
Six Flags Magic Mountain
                          Another Death Linked to X2 Coaster
body:
Six Flags Magic Mountain
                          Another Death Linked to X2 Coaster
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 18, 2026
                            8:45 AM PST
                                                                            
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Another death, more brain injuries, and years of warning signs ... a bombshell investigation is putting Six Flags Magic Mountain's X2 roller coaster and California safety regulators under the microscope.
      
    
              According to a joint investigation by ProPublica and L.A. Material, 17-year-old Christopher Gibson died in June after riding the extreme coaster during a high school graduation trip with his mother.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              The teen complained of a severe headache after visiting the park and was later found unresponsive in their hotel room. An autopsy determined he died from blunt force head trauma, though investigators haven't conclusively linked his death to a specific ride.
      

              Here's where things get troubling ... a homicide detective alerted California safety regulators in early July that Christopher's death could be connected to the park. The detective reportedly didn't receive a response until nearly two months later.
      
    
              Six Flags tells TMZ ... "Safety is our ethos and is at the heart of everything we do. Six Flags has a comprehensive, multilayered safety and inspection program that includes documented daily inspections before opening each day, ongoing preventive maintenance and additional internal and external oversight. That oversight includes independent third-party ride inspection firms, insurance and state inspectors where applicable and Six Flags corporate engineering and safety professionals."
      
    
              They continue, "X2 consistently passed a multitude of safety tests throughout its nearly 20 years of operation. Magic Mountain's investigation and analysis of the ride remain ongoing. We are fully cooperating with Cal/OSHA."
      
    
              Meanwhile, two more riders suffered serious brain injuries after riding X2 that July.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
              And this apparently wasn't the first warning sign ... the investigation found at least 70 reported head injuries involving X2 since 2010, with regulators frequently conducting little or no investigation.
      
    
              In more than 35 cases, officials blamed riders for failing to position their heads correctly.
      
    
              Six Flags says X2 consistently passed safety tests and insists safety remains its priority. California regulators say their investigation is ongoing.
      
    
              The coaster has since been permanently closed ... but the disturbing question remains whether earlier action could have prevented further injuries.

FAA
                          Greenlit the Upgrade That Grounded America?!?
body:
FAA
                          Greenlit the Upgrade That Grounded America?!?
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 18, 2026
                            6:41 AM PST
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              The Federal Aviation Administration may have some explaining to do over last week's nationwide flight meltdown ... 'cause it turns out the agency reportedly gave the green light to the very work that preceded the massive shutdown.
      
    
              According to The Washington Post, an FAA official was on-site in El Dorado, Arkansas, Friday as contractor L3Harris Technologies switched critical air traffic communications from aging copper wires to fiber-optic cables.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
              And here's the kicker ... the official reportedly tested the new equipment and signed off on the job. Just eight minutes later, air traffic control communications began failing across much of the country.
      

              The new details complicate the blame game surrounding the massive outage ... with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy repeatedly pointing the finger at L3Harris, even questioning whether the company's work was incompetent.
      
    
              But a person familiar with the investigation told the Post the criticism was "inflammatory" and "insulting" ... arguing the FAA was involved every step of the way, including approving the work before it began.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
              The source says everything appeared to be working properly when the job was completed ... and investigators still haven't determined exactly what went wrong.
      
    
              As TMZ previously reported, the FAA ordered a rare nationwide ground stop Friday after communications failures disrupted air traffic control operations ... leaving travelers stranded and flights grounded for roughly 4 ½ hours.
      
    
              We've also reported the FBI is involved in the investigation ... with the equipment being examined at an L3Harris facility in Florida under FAA supervision.
      
    
              Meanwhile, L3Harris has reportedly stopped using the type of router implicated in the outage while continuing its broader modernization work.
      
    
              So, while Duffy has been pointing fingers at the contractor ... the latest revelations suggest the FAA may have played a bigger role than previously understood.
